newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil holds symbolic trial over peasant massacres.
newsitem.headline: Brazil holds symbolic trial over peasant massacres.

text.p: Survivors of two massacres of Brazilian peasants told chilling tales of their ordeals at the hands of police before a symbolic international trial of two state governments on Thursday.

"I rolled around on the floor; I covered myself with blood and I pretended to be one of the dead," said Moacir Camargo Ferreira of a clash between landless farmers and police in October 1995 which left nine peasants and two policemen dead.

In the absence of a formal trial of police officers involved in that massacre in Rondonia state and another in April, when 19 peasants were killed in Para, human rights activists and lawyers called for a symbolic trial.
Its aim, organisers said, was "to denounce the crimes by agents of the Brazilian state and draw up recommendations for establishing peace and justice."
Among those presiding at the event were Phillipe Texier, a French judge who sits on the International Commission on Human Rights, and Portuguese novelist Jose Saramago.
Dozens of landless farmers, carrying their distinctive red flags, packed a hall in Congress to hear the views of experts.

"I have no doubt that there was a massacre in Para," said Nelson Massini, a forensic scientist from Rio de Janeiro's Federal University who carried out autopsies on the 19 victims and showed gruesome images of corpses with bullet holes and wounds from agricultural tools.

Of 34 identified bullet wounds, 17 were located in the heads of the victims and many others were to the heart. Others had been caused by weapons fired at point-blank range, including some to the nape of the neck, he said.
"There were executions and there was a massacre because the number of dead is excessive (and) there are no fatal victims on the police side," Massini said.

A defence lawyer representing the states of Rondonia and Para, which are responsible for their respective police forces, argued that blame for the massacres lay with the federal government's delay in implementing its land reform programme.

The Landless Movement, which encourages peasants to take over unused farmland, claims that 4.8 million Brazilian families need land. The Catholic Church's Pastoral Land Commission recently reported that 90 people have been killed in fighting over land in the last two years.
